To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a 73‐ year‐old woman with a metastatic breast carcinoma developed interfollicu lar Hodgkin's disease in the right cervical lymph node.

we have reported a 73‐y‐old woman with metastatic breast cancer who developed interfolliicular Hodgkin's disease in the right cervical lymph node, which was a 'collision tumour' with the breast carcinoma.
we report a case of collision tumor in which the components were metastatic breast cancer and interfollicular HD in a patient with progressive metastatic breast carcinoma.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the clinical and pathologic features of a collision tumor in the lymph nodes of a patient with metastatic breast carcinoma and Hodgkin's disease.
the clinical, pathological, and therapeutic aspects of the coexistence of Hodgkin's disease with metastatic carcinoma in the lymph nodes.
a rare case of collision tumor in which metastatic carcinoma and Hodgkin's disease were present simultaneously.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this patient had two independent neoplastic diseases that were coincident in the cervical lymph nodes.
this case is an example of a collision tumor, and not an example of a Hodgkin's disease arising in the background of a pre‐existent metastatic breast carcinoma.
this is an unusual case in which a patient with metastatic breast cancer also developed Hodgkin's disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Hodgkin's disease is a disease of the immune system and the breast cancer is a disease of epithelial cells, which is why the two tumors are not usually found together.
the coexistence and order of appearance of these two pathologies in this case remain unknown.
this is the first reported case of a collision tumor between Hodgkin's disease, and metastatic breast adenocarcinoma.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the diagnosis of collision tumors should not be excluded in the presence of two or more neoplasms with different histological characteristics in the same tissue, even if they appear to be separated.
the coexistence of Hodgkin's disease with another malignancy is not a rare event.
the co‐occurrence of Hodgkin's disease, and breast carcinoma in the same patient is extremely rare.
